**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my indecision. A thousand words—what a strange, arbitrary number. A thousand steps could take you anywhere: across a city, up a mountain, or in circles around your own kitchen at 3 AM, wondering where it all went wrong. Words are like that, too. They can build bridges or burn them. They can be weapons, balm, or just noise in the void.

I think about the first time I realized words had power. I was eight, and my teacher had us write letters to ourselves to open in ten years. I don’t remember what I wrote, but I remember the weight of the envelope in my hands, the way sealing it felt like locking a piece of my soul in a time capsule. Would that kid recognize me now? Would they be proud? Disappointed? Words outlive us, in a way. They linger in emails, in marginalia, in half-forgotten texts. They’re ghosts of who we were when we wrote them.

A thousand words is a short story, a rant, a love letter, a eulogy. It’s the length of a bad breakup explained in excruciating detail to a friend who’s nodding but checking their watch. It’s the monologue of a villain just before the hero kicks them into a pit. It’s the quiet confession you delete before hitting send.

I wonder how many words I’ve wasted. The apologies I didn’t mean, the promises I couldn’t keep, the jokes that landed like lead balloons. The times I said *nothing* when I should have said *everything*. Silence is its own kind of word, heavy with subtext. A paused text thread. A door left unknocked. The space between "I love you" and "…but."

Then there are the words that change things. "You’re hired." "It’s malignant." "I do." Three syllables can alter the trajectory of a life. A thousand words could rewrite history if they found the right ears. But most words don’t. Most words dissolve into the static, lost in the hum of a million other voices saying the same things: *I’m tired. I’m lonely. Does this mean anything?*

Maybe that’s the magic. We keep trying anyway. We carve our initials into desks, scribble poems on napkins, scream into the internet void. We write even when no one’s listening, because the act itself is a rebellion against entropy. Words are proof we were here, that we *felt* something, even if it was just boredom or hunger or the ache of a Tuesday afternoon.

I’m at 500 words now. Halfway. The page is no longer blank, but it’s not full either. Like most things in life—half-empty or half-full, depending on the day. I could fill the rest with a story about a woman who collects lost gloves, or a manifesto about why pineapple belongs on pizza, or a step-by-step guide to folding a fitted sheet (spoiler: it’s impossible). But maybe the point isn’t what the words *are*, but that they *exist* at all.

Here’s a secret: I don’t know what I’m doing. None of us do, really. We’re all just stringing words together like Christmas lights, hoping the circuit connects, that the bulbs will glow. Sometimes they do. Sometimes you get a sad, flickering strand that makes the whole thing look cheaper than it is.

But here’s another secret: that’s okay. The imperfect words are the real ones. The messy, honest, half-formed thoughts—they’re the ones that matter. The ones that say, *I don’t have it figured out, but I’m here, and I’m trying.*

I’ve got 200 words left. Let’s make them count.

To the person reading this: Hello. I don’t know you, but I’m glad you’re here. Maybe you’re procrastinating, or lonely, or just killing time. Maybe you needed to hear that it’s okay to not have all the answers. That your words matter, even the ones you’re afraid to say out loud. That you’re allowed to take up space, to be loud or quiet or somewhere in between.

And to the eight-year-old me, wherever they are in the timeline of my life: I hope you’re proud. I’m still figuring it out, but I’m trying. I’m using my words.

(998. Close enough.)
